title: What is the Kafka controller broker (one elected broker managing partition leader elections and broker join/leave), and how does leader election from the ISR (in-sync replicas) keep a partition available when its leader broker fails?
shortTitle: What is the Kafka controller broker, and how does leader election from the ISR keep a partition available when its leader broker fails?

s1_definition.profdef: The controller is a single broker in the cluster, elected to a special coordinating role, that manages cluster-wide metadata: it detects brokers joining and leaving, tracks partition leadership and the in-sync replica set per partition, and drives leader elections. When a broker that leads some partitions fails, the controller notices the broker is gone and, for each partition that lost its leader, elects a new leader from that partition's in-sync replicas, the replicas known to be fully caught up, then propagates the updated metadata so clients redirect to the new leaders. Because the new leader comes from the in-sync set, it already has all committed data, so the partition stays available and no acknowledged data is lost.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has many branches, and for each type of account one branch is the designated master that handles all transactions while backup branches keep live copies. The bank also appoints one head-office coordinator whose job is to know which branches are up, which branch is master for each account, and which backups are fully up to date. If the master branch for an account suddenly burns down, the coordinator immediately picks one of the fully-up-to-date backup branches to become the new master and updates the central directory so tellers everywhere start routing that account's transactions to the new master. Because the chosen backup was fully caught up, customers lose nothing and service continues almost without interruption. That head-office coordinator is the controller, and choosing only from fully-caught-up backups is leader election from the in-sync replicas.
s1_definition.oneliner: The controller is the one elected broker that manages broker membership and partition leadership, and on a leader's failure it elects a new leader from the partition's in-sync replicas, which already hold all committed data, so the partition stays available with no acknowledged data lost.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The controller is a single broker in the cluster, elected to a special coordinating role, that manages cluster-wide metadata: it detects brokers joining and leaving, tracks partition leadership and the in-sync replica set per partition, and drives leader elections. When a broker that leads some partitions fails, the controller notices the broker is gone and, for each partition that lost its leader, elects a new leader from that partition's in-sync replicas, the replicas known to be fully caught up, then propagates the updated metadata so clients redirect to the new leaders. Because the new leader comes from the in-sync set, it already has all committed data, so the partition stays available and no acknowledged data is lost.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has many branches, and for each type of account one branch is the designated master that handles all transactions while backup branches keep live copies. The bank also appoints one head-office coordinator whose job is to know which branches are up, which branch is master for each account, and which backups are fully up to date. If the master branch for an account suddenly burns down, the coordinator immediately picks one of the fully-up-to-date backup branches to become the new master and updates the central directory so tellers everywhere start routing that account's transactions to the new master. Because the chosen backup was fully caught up, customers lose nothing and service continues almost without interruption. That head-office coordinator is the controller, and choosing only from fully-caught-up backups is leader election from the in-sync replicas.

**One line to remember:** The controller is the one elected broker that manages broker membership and partition leadership, and on a leader's failure it elects a new leader from the partition's in-sync replicas, which already hold all committed data, so the partition stays available with no acknowledged data lost.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with what the controller is and how it is chosen. Exactly one broker in the cluster acts as the controller at any time. In older Kafka this election was coordinated through ZooKeeper, and in modern Kafka it is handled by the KRaft metadata quorum, a built-in Raft-based consensus among a set of controller nodes that elects an active controller and stores cluster metadata in an internal metadata log. Either way the outcome is the same: there is a single active controller responsible for cluster-wide decisions, and if the controller itself fails, a new controller is elected so the role is always filled.

Next, what the controller does. It maintains the authoritative cluster metadata: the list of live brokers, the replica assignment for every partition, which replica is the leader of each partition, and the in-sync replica set for each partition. It watches for brokers joining and leaving. When a broker registers, the controller updates metadata and may assign it work; when a broker's session expires or it stops heartbeating, the controller marks it dead. The controller also drives leadership changes, including the routine preferred-leader rebalancing and the critical failover on broker failure, and it pushes metadata updates out so every broker and client learns the current leaders.

Now the in-sync replica set, which is the heart of safe failover. Each partition has a leader and some followers, and the in-sync replica set is the subset of replicas, always including the leader, that are fully caught up with the leader within the allowed lag window governed by replica lag time. A follower that keeps up stays in the in-sync set; one that falls behind is removed from it until it catches up. A record is considered committed only once it has been replicated to all members of the in-sync set, so every in-sync replica is guaranteed to hold every committed record. This is precisely why the in-sync set is the safe pool to elect from.

Here is the failover sequence when a leader broker fails. The controller detects the broker is gone, through a lost session or missed heartbeats. For every partition that broker was leading, the controller looks at that partition's in-sync replica set, excludes the dead broker, and elects one of the remaining in-sync replicas as the new leader. It updates the metadata to record the new leader and the new in-sync set, and propagates that to the cluster. Clients that were talking to the dead leader get a NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION error, refresh metadata, discover the new leader, and resume. Because the new leader was in-sync, it already has all committed records, so consumers continue from where they were and no acknowledged write is lost. The partition is unavailable only for the brief window between failure detection and the new leader being published.

The crucial safety rule is unclean leader election. If a partition's entire in-sync set is on brokers that are all down, the controller faces a choice: wait for an in-sync replica to come back, preserving correctness but staying unavailable, or elect an out-of-sync replica that is missing some committed records, restoring availability but losing data. This is controlled by `unclean.leader.election.enable`. For a bank you keep it false, so the controller will never elect a stale replica and will instead wait, trading availability for the guarantee that no acknowledged data is silently lost. Combined with replication factor three, acks all, and minimum in-sync replicas of two, this gives you a partition that tolerates one broker failure with zero data loss and near-continuous availability.

Senior-level nuances. The failover speed depends on how quickly the controller detects the failure, which is governed by session and heartbeat timeouts, so there is a tension between fast failover and not evicting briefly slow brokers. The modern KRaft design removes the ZooKeeper dependency and makes controller failover and metadata propagation faster and more scalable, which matters for large clusters with many partitions. The controller is a single logical decision-maker but is itself made fault-tolerant, by ZooKeeper-based re-election in the old world or by the Raft controller quorum in KRaft, so there is no permanent single point of failure. And the in-sync set is dynamic, so the pool of eligible new leaders shrinks under load or during churn, which is another reason to keep brokers stable and to alert on in-sync set shrink, because a partition sitting at an in-sync set of one has no safe failover target left.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs a three-broker cluster. The `settlements` topic has replication factor three, acks all, and minimum in-sync replicas two, and its partition zero is led by broker-1 with followers on broker-2 and broker-3, all in-sync. Rajesh and Priya settlements flow through it.

Problem 1 — broker-1 suffers a hardware failure. Without a controller and in-sync election, settlement would stop for that partition. This is where the controller detects the failure and elects a new leader from the in-sync set so settlements continue.

Problem 2 — the team wanted to be certain no acknowledged settlement could be lost during failover and that an out-of-date replica could never be promoted. This is the unclean leader election guard, kept false, and the reason the new leader is only ever chosen from the in-sync set.

Our runnable demo models a `Controller` tracking brokers, leadership, and the in-sync set per partition, `Broker` objects that can fail, and a `Partition` with a leader and an in-sync set. We fail the leader, have the controller elect a new in-sync leader, verify committed data is intact, then demonstrate the unclean-election guard when the whole in-sync set is down. The classes are `ControllerFailoverDemo`, `Broker`, `Partition`, and `Controller`.

```bash
# Run it

# Confirm durability + safe-failover settings on the topic
kafka-configs.sh --describe --topic settlements --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 \
  | grep -E 'min.insync.replicas|unclean.leader.election'
kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic settlements --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092  # shows Leader, Replicas, Isr

# Run the demo (leader fails -> ISR election; whole ISR fails -> safe wait)
javac demo/ControllerFailoverDemo.java -d out
java -cp out com.bank.controller.demo.ControllerFailoverDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a three-broker cluster, partition settlements-0 led by broker-1 with broker-2 and broker-3 in-sync, holding ten thousand committed settlement records.

Step 1: The controller, the single elected coordinating broker, holds the authoritative metadata: broker-1 leads settlements-0, and the in-sync set is broker-1, broker-2, and broker-3. Every in-sync replica holds all ten thousand committed records because a record is only committed once all in-sync replicas have it.

Step 2: Broker-1 fails. The controller detects this through a lost session or missed heartbeats and marks broker-1 dead, removing it from the in-sync set of every partition it belonged to.

Step 3: For settlements-0, which just lost its leader, the controller elects a new leader strictly from the surviving in-sync replicas, broker-2 or broker-3. It picks one, say broker-2, updates the metadata to record the new leader and the new in-sync set, and propagates it to the cluster.

Step 4: Settlement producers and consumers that were talking to broker-1 get NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION, refresh metadata, learn broker-2 is the new leader, and resume. Because broker-2 was in-sync, it already holds all ten thousand committed records, so consumers continue seamlessly and no acknowledged settlement is lost. The partition was unavailable only for the brief detect-and-elect window.

Step 5: In the extreme case where broker-2 and broker-3 also fail, leaving no in-sync replica, the controller faces the unclean-election choice. Because unclean leader election is disabled for this bank topic, it refuses to promote an out-of-sync replica that might be missing committed records, and instead leaves the partition unavailable until an in-sync replica returns. This keeps correctness absolute, trading availability for the guarantee that no acknowledged settlement is ever silently lost.

Final output:

```
[2026-10-25 03:10:55] [INFO] === Leader broker-1 fails ===
[2026-10-25 03:10:55] [INFO] Controller elected new leader broker-2 from ISR [broker-2, broker-3] (no committed data lost)
[2026-10-25 03:10:55] [INFO] New leader of settlements-0 = broker-2, committed records intact = 10000 (new leader was in-sync)
[2026-10-25 03:10:55] [INFO] === All remaining ISR fail (broker-2, broker-3) ===
[2026-10-25 03:10:55] [WARNING] No in-sync replica available; unclean election disabled -> partition UNAVAILABLE but correct, waiting for an ISR member to return
[2026-10-25 03:10:55] [INFO] Leader now = NONE (waiting) (unclean election disabled -> wait, stay correct)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Controller (single elected broker) holds cluster metadata:
    settlements-0: leader=broker-1, ISR={broker-1,broker-2,broker-3}, committed=10000
    │
    ▼ broker-1 FAILS (lost session / missed heartbeats)
  Controller detects failure
    │ remove broker-1 from ISR -> ISR={broker-2,broker-3}
    ▼ elect new leader FROM ISR (holds all committed data)
  new leader = broker-2  ── propagate metadata ──→ all brokers + clients
    │
    ▼ clients hit old leader -> NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION -> refresh -> resume on broker-2
  partition AVAILABLE again, 10000 records intact, NO acknowledged data lost

  Extreme: ISR becomes empty
    ├─ unclean.leader.election = false -> WAIT (unavailable but correct)  [bank default]
    └─ unclean.leader.election = true  -> promote stale replica (AVAILABLE but DATA LOSS)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The controller is a single broker elected to a special coordinating role for the whole cluster. It holds the authoritative metadata, the list of live brokers, the replica assignment and current leader for every partition, and the in-sync replica set per partition, and it is responsible for detecting brokers joining and leaving and for driving leader elections. In older Kafka the controller was coordinated through ZooKeeper, and in modern Kafka it is handled by the KRaft Raft-based controller quorum, but either way there is always exactly one active controller, and it is itself made fault-tolerant through re-election, so it is not a permanent single point of failure.

The mechanism that keeps a partition available when its leader fails is leader election from the in-sync replica set. Each partition has a leader and followers, and the in-sync set is the subset of replicas, always including the leader, that are fully caught up within the allowed lag window. A record is only considered committed once every in-sync replica has it, which means every in-sync replica is guaranteed to hold every committed record. That guarantee is exactly why the in-sync set is the safe pool to elect from.

So when a broker that leads some partitions fails, the controller detects it through a lost session or missed heartbeats, removes it from the in-sync sets, and for each partition that lost its leader it elects a new leader strictly from the surviving in-sync replicas. It updates and propagates the metadata, clients talking to the dead leader get a not-leader error, refresh metadata, find the new leader, and resume. Because the new leader was in-sync, it already has all committed data, so consumers continue seamlessly and no acknowledged write is lost; the partition is unavailable only for the brief window between failure detection and the new leader being published. On the National Bank of India settlements topic, with replication factor three, acks all, and minimum in-sync replicas two, losing broker-1 simply promotes broker-2 from the in-sync set and settlements for Rajesh and Priya keep flowing with every committed record intact.

The crucial safety rule I always call out is unclean leader election. If a partition's entire in-sync set is down, the controller must choose between waiting for an in-sync replica to return, which stays correct but unavailable, and promoting an out-of-sync replica that is missing committed records, which restores availability but loses data. For a bank I keep unclean leader election disabled, so the controller will never promote a stale replica and will instead wait, trading availability for the absolute guarantee that no acknowledged data is silently lost. The nuances I add are that failover speed depends on the session and heartbeat timeouts, so there is a tension between fast detection and not evicting briefly slow brokers; that KRaft makes controller failover and metadata propagation faster and more scalable than the old ZooKeeper design; and that I alert on in-sync set shrink, because a partition sitting at an in-sync set of one has no safe failover target left. The one-line principle is that the controller plus in-sync election is how Kafka turns a broker failure into a quick, lossless leadership handoff rather than an outage.

keyPoints: Replication factor: copies of each partition across brokers
ISR (In-Sync Replicas): followers caught up with leader
acks=all: wait for all ISR to acknowledge — strongest durability
